q: With noUncheckedIndexedAccess on, what is the type of first?
code:
declare const orders: Order[];
const first = orders[0];
options: Order
Order | null
Order | undefined
Readonly<Order> | undefined
explain: The array may be empty, so reading an index can give undefined; measured, assigning it to a non-optional variable fails with TS2322. Without the flag the type is Order, which is the lie the flag exists to remove. Nothing in JavaScript returns null for a missing index.

q: types.ts exports an interface Order and a constant x. Without verbatimModuleSyntax, main.ts does import { Order, x } from './types.ts'. What happens with node main.ts on Node 24?
options: It crashes at startup: the module does not provide an export named Order
It runs, because Node sees that Order is only used as a type and drops it
It runs, and Order is undefined wherever the code reads it as a value
Node reports a type error on Order and exits before running anything
explain: Measured: SyntaxError: The requested module './types.ts' does not provide an export named 'Order'. Node only strips type syntax; an import without type is kept as a value import, and interfaces do not exist at runtime. Node never type-checks, so it cannot know Order is a type; verbatimModuleSyntax reports TS1484 at compile time instead.

q: Which of these files runs with node file.ts on Node 24, without extra flags?
options: One with enum Status { Draft, Paid } used to tag order rows
One with a class using constructor(private readonly url: string)
One with namespace Billing { export const vat = 0.2; } for tax rates
One with a union type, satisfies and a type-only declare namespace
explain: Node strips erasable syntax only. Measured: enums, parameter properties and namespaces with code all fail with ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX because they generate JavaScript. Types, satisfies and a type-only declare namespace disappear entirely, so that file ran.

q: Which statement about TypeScript 7.0 is correct as of October 2026?
options: It is a preview only, published as @typescript/native-preview until 7.1 is out
It is the stable typescript package, run as tsc, with no programmatic API yet
It adds a tsgo command that replaces tsc and accepts every 6.0 option
It is a runtime that executes TypeScript and replaces Node's type stripping
explain: TypeScript 7.0 was released on 8 July 2026; npm shows typescript 7.0.2, and the announcement says it “does not ship with an API”, with a new one planned for 7.1. The native preview package was the pre-release channel. Options deprecated in 6.0 are removed in 7.0, and it is a compiler, not a runtime.

q: toResponseBody(order: PublicOrder) returns JSON.stringify(order), where PublicOrder has id, status and totalCents. It is called with a database row held in a variable, which also has paymentToken. What happens?
options: Compile error: paymentToken does not exist in PublicOrder
It compiles and the JSON contains paymentToken
It compiles and TypeScript removes paymentToken from the output
It compiles but throws at runtime
explain: Structural typing only requires the fields the type asks for, and types do not exist at runtime to remove anything; measured on Node 24, the token was in the JSON. The excess property error (TS2353) applies only to an object literal written directly at that spot, not to a variable holding a row.

q: applyOrderEvent ends its switch (event.type) with default: return assertNever(event);. A colleague adds { type: 'partial_refund'; at: Date } to OrderEvent but no case. What happens?
options: Partial refunds fall into default and throw at runtime only
Nothing visible until the first partial refund reaches the service
tsc fails at assertNever(event): partial_refund is not assignable to never
tsc fails on the OrderEvent declaration, which has an unhandled member
explain: Once the handled cases are removed, event still contains the partial_refund member, which cannot go into a never parameter: measured TS2345. The runtime throw in assertNever is only a backup; the point is that the build fails first. The union type itself is perfectly valid.

q: With the typed EventBus of the lesson, and orderId, paymentId, totalCents and amountCents variables of the right branded types, which call compiles?
options: bus.emit('order.paid', { orderId, totalCents })
bus.emit('order.payed', { orderId, paymentId })
bus.on('order.placed', async (event) => audit.log(event.paymentId))
bus.emit('order.refunded', { orderId, amountCents })
explain: The name constrains the payload through DomainEvents[E]. Measured: the first call passes a totalCents that an order.paid payload does not have (TS2353) and misses paymentId, the misspelled name is not in keyof DomainEvents (TS2345), and an order.placed payload has no paymentId (TS2339). The refunded event has exactly the required fields.

q: With OrderId and PaymentId branded as in the lesson, which line compiles?
options: const text: string = toOrderId('ord_1');
loadOrder('ord_' + order.number);
loadOrder(refund.paymentId);
const id: OrderId = 'ord_' + crypto.randomUUID();
explain: A branded value is a string plus a compile-time marker, so it can be used as a string. The other direction is blocked: measured, a plain string or a PaymentId passed as an OrderId fails with TS2345. Only the checking function, with its single as OrderId, creates one.

q: const routes = { home: '/', orders: '/orders' } satisfies Record<string, string>; What is the type of routes.orders?
options: '/orders'
string
string | undefined
Record<string, string>
explain: Measured: assigning routes.orders to a '/orders' variable fails, so the literal widened to string, because the target type asks for string. The keys stay known, so there is no undefined, unlike an annotation with noUncheckedIndexedAccess. as const satisfies would keep '/orders'.

q: A client posts { customerId: 'cus_1', items: [...], isAdmin: true } to POST /orders, which uses PlaceOrderBody.safeParse(req.body), built with z.object and no isAdmin field. What is in parsed.data?
options: Every field, isAdmin included
Nothing: success is false because of the unknown key
Every field except isAdmin
isAdmin set to undefined
explain: Measured with Zod 4.6.7: success was true and isAdmin was absent, because z.object strips unknown keys. That protects against mass assignment. Rejecting the request is what z.strictObject does (issue code unrecognized_keys).

q: The Orders API calls the payment provider through a client generated with openapi-typescript and openapi-fetch. What do the generated types guarantee at runtime?
options: That responses match the spec, because openapi-fetch validates each body against it
That the provider cannot change its contract without breaking your build first
That 4xx and 5xx responses are thrown as typed exceptions you can catch
Nothing at runtime: responses are typed from the spec but never checked
explain: Generated types are compile-time only; the docs describe data and error typed from the spec, not validated. If the provider sends something else, your code receives it. For an API you do not control, parse the response with a schema. openapi-fetch returns errors in error; it does not throw them.

q: With strict on, what does tsc say about catch (error) { console.log(error.message); }?
options: 'error' is of type 'unknown' (TS18046)
Nothing: error is typed Error
Nothing: error is typed any
That catch needs an explicit type annotation
explain: strict includes useUnknownInCatchVariables, because JavaScript can throw any value, a string included. Measured: TS18046. Narrow first with error instanceof Error. It was any before that flag, which is what older code still assumes.

q: This helper merges the options of the delivery partner's HTTP client. What does it print, and which flag would have refused the call?
options: { timeoutMs: 5000, retries: 2 }; no flag needed, the spread skips undefined values
{ timeoutMs: undefined, retries: 2 }; strictNullChecks
{ timeoutMs: undefined, retries: 2 }; exactOptionalPropertyTypes
{ timeoutMs: 5000, retries: 2 }; noUncheckedIndexedAccess
explain: Measured: a key present with the value undefined overwrites the default in a spread, so the client ends up with no timeout. exactOptionalPropertyTypes makes timeoutMs?: number mean “absent or a number” and rejects the call (TS2379). strictNullChecks alone accepts it, because an optional property normally allows undefined.

q: A team wants to drop the build step of its NestJS service and run node src/main.ts in production on Node 24. Their tsconfig has erasableSyntaxOnly and tsc passes. What do you tell them?
options: It works: erasableSyntaxOnly guarantees Node can strip the code
It fails on the decorators, which tsc accepts under that flag; keep a tsc or SWC build
It works once they add a reflect-metadata import at the top of main.ts
It works, but startup is slower because Node type-checks first
explain: Measured: a decorated class compiled cleanly under erasableSyntaxOnly, then failed in Node with SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token. NestJS also needs emitDecoratorMetadata for dependency injection, which only a real compiler (tsc, or SWC through the Nest CLI) produces. Node never type-checks.

q: In a pnpm monorepo, @acme/contracts exports ./index.ts and the Orders API runs it unbuilt with Node 24 type stripping. It works locally. After the package is published to the private registry and installed in another repo, startup fails. Why?
options: Node will not strip types under node_modules; the workspace link pointed outside it
The registry removes .ts files from published packages unless files lists them
pnpm compiles workspace packages on install, and a registry install skips that step
The consuming repo lacks rewriteRelativeImportExtensions in its tsconfig
explain: Measured: a linked workspace package ran because Node follows the link to the real path, while a .ts file inside node_modules failed with ERR_UNSUPPORTED_NODE_MODULES_TYPE_STRIPPING. A published package must ship compiled JavaScript. tsconfig flags do not matter to Node, which ignores tsconfig.

q: A service uses tsx watch locally and an esbuild bundle in production. A pull request that passes null to a function expecting a string was merged and crashed in production. Which fix do you ship?
options: Replace esbuild with tsdown, which type-checks every file while it bundles
Switch the dev loop from tsx to node --watch src/main.ts, which checks types
Add a CI step running tsc --noEmit that blocks the merge on errors
Turn on strict in tsconfig so that esbuild rejects type errors
explain: tsx documents that it does not type-check (measured: const s: string = 42 ran), and esbuild and tsdown transform code without checking it; Node's type stripping does not check either. Only tsc (6.0 or 7.0) checks types, so it must run in CI. tsconfig flags change what tsc reports, not what a bundler does.

q: Your backend monorepo wants TypeScript 7's speed in CI, but it uses type-aware lint rules that call the TypeScript API. What is the plan the TypeScript team recommends?
options: Wait for 7.1, because 7.0 cannot type-check a project that also runs a type-aware linter
Install 7.0 everywhere and turn the type-aware lint rules off until they are rewritten
Stay on 6.0 only, because 7.0 dropped module: nodenext along with node10
Use 7.0 for tsc and keep 6.0 beside it via @typescript/typescript6 for lint
explain: The 7.0 announcement says it ships no API yet and describes installing @typescript/typescript6 (command tsc6) next to 7.0 for tools that need the 6.0 API. Waiting is not required: the type check itself works on 7.0. nodenext is supported; it is node10 resolution that was removed.

q: What is the risk in this webhook code?
options: The predicate checks one key but claims a full RefundEvent, and the compiler trusts it
It does not compile: the in operator cannot be used on a value typed unknown
value is RefundEvent makes TypeScript insert a runtime check of every field
None: after typeof value === 'object' the compiler has proven the shape
explain: A type predicate is a promise the compiler does not verify: once it returns true, body is a full RefundEvent everywhere. Any object with a type key passes, so refund(undefined, undefined) can run. Use a schema (RefundEvent.safeParse) for anything beyond one field. The in check does compile after the object and null checks.

q: Using the lesson's applyOrderEvent, what happens with applyOrderEvent(pendingOrder, { type: 'refund', at: new Date() }), where pendingOrder has status: 'pending_payment'?
options: It returns a refunded order with refundedAt set to the event date
It returns the pending order unchanged and logs nothing
It throws InvalidTransitionError: only paid orders can be refunded
It does not compile: a pending order cannot be passed with a refund event
explain: The refund case only returns when order.status === 'paid'; otherwise it breaks out of the switch and reaches the throw. Measured on Node 24: “Cannot refund an order that is pending_payment”. The parameter types allow any pair of order and event, so this rule is checked at runtime, in one place.

q: A reviewer proposes replacing default: return assertNever(event); with default: return order; “to be safe”. What do you answer?
options: Agreed: returning the order unchanged avoids crashes in production
Refuse: a new event type would then compile and be silently ignored
It makes no difference: tsc checks exhaustiveness on every switch anyway
Agreed, as long as noFallthroughCasesInSwitch is enabled in the tsconfig
explain: With a value-returning default, event is never required to be never: measured, adding a partial_refund event then compiled without an error, and those events would be dropped without a trace. tsc does not check exhaustiveness by itself: the never assignment is what creates the check. noFallthroughCasesInSwitch is about cases without break, not about missing ones.

q: With Express 5 and @types/express, what does tsc report for this route?
options: Nothing: req.params is a Record<string, string> for every route
Both properties are string | undefined under noUncheckedIndexedAccess
An error on orderId, because route params must be validated before use
TS2339 on customerId: the route string is parsed into the params type
explain: The Express types use template literal types to read :orderId out of the route string, so req.params is { orderId: string }. Measured with @types/express 5.0.6: TS2339 on customerId only. A plain dictionary type would be the case if the route were a variable of type string.

q: What is AggregateOf<'order.placed' | 'payment.captured'>?
code:
type AggregateOf<Name extends string> =
  Name extends `${infer Aggregate}.${string}` ? Aggregate : never;
options: never, because a union does not extend the pattern
'order' | 'payment'
string
'order.placed' | 'payment.captured'
explain: A conditional type on a naked type parameter is distributive: it runs once per union member and joins the results. Measured: 'order' and 'payment' are accepted and 'placed' is rejected (TS2322). never would be the result for a name without a dot.

q: A checkout converts a price string with Number(price) * 100 before saving integer cents. For '19.99', what does Node 24 compute, and what do you change?
options: 1999; nothing to change, doubles are exact up to two decimal places
1999, because V8 rounds every multiplication result to 15 significant digits
1998.9999999999998; convert the decimal string to exact integer cents at the edge
1998.9999999999998; store it in a double precision column instead of an integer
explain: Measured: 19.99 * 100 is 1998.9999999999998, because 19.99 has no exact binary representation. Truncating it gives 1998 cents, a lost cent per item. Convert once, at the edge, to an exact integer, then compute in integer cents; floating-point columns only move the problem.

q: A developer wants enum OrderStatus { PendingPayment = 'pending_payment', Paid = 'paid' } in the Orders API, which runs under Node 24 type stripping with erasableSyntaxOnly. What do you propose?
options: A const enum, because tsc inlines its values and erases the declaration
Keep the enum and start production with --experimental-transform-types
A namespace OrderStatus holding one exported constant per status
An as const object plus a union type derived from its values
explain: The as const object gives runtime values, readable strings in JSON and logs, and a union type through (typeof OrderStatus)[keyof typeof OrderStatus], all erasable. Measured: a const enum is rejected too, with TS1294 under the flag and ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX in Node. Namespaces with code fail the same way, and the transform flag printed an ExperimentalWarning on Node 24.11 and no longer exists in Node 26.

q: Why write const retryPolicies = { … } satisfies Record<string, RetryPolicy> rather than const retryPolicies: Record<string, RetryPolicy> = { … }?
options: Only satisfies keeps the known keys, so retryPolicies.paymentProvider is never undefined
Only satisfies catches backoff: 'fixd'; the annotation accepts any string there
satisfies also freezes the object at runtime, like Object.freeze
satisfies makes every nested property readonly, like as const
explain: Both forms check the value against the type (measured TS2820 on 'fixd' with satisfies). The difference is the variable's type: the annotation turns it into a Record, so under noUncheckedIndexedAccess every lookup is possibly undefined (TS18048); satisfies keeps the inferred shape. It is a type-level operator: nothing happens at runtime.

q: The env schema has PORT: z.coerce.number().int().default(3000), with no .min. A deploy sets PORT= (empty). What value does the service get?
options: 3000, because an empty string counts as missing
A validation error: an empty string is not a number
0, because Number('') is 0
NaN, rejected by .int()
explain: Measured with Zod 4.6.7: z.coerce.number() turned '' into 0. The default only applies to undefined, not to an empty string, and Number('') is 0, not NaN. Listening on port 0 lets the OS pick a random port, so the service starts and nobody can reach it; add .min(1).

q: Your service validates tRPC 11 procedure inputs with Zod. An edge function team wants Valibot 1.5 for its smaller bundles. What changes on the tRPC side?
options: Nothing specific: Valibot implements Standard Schema, which tRPC accepts
tRPC needs a Valibot adapter package, the same way it needed one for Zod
Valibot schemas must first be converted to Zod with a code generation step in CI
tRPC only accepts Zod schemas, so the edge team has to keep Zod
explain: Standard Schema is a shared interface: a ~standard property with version, vendor and validate. Zod 4.6.7, Valibot 1.5.0 and ArkType 2.2.9 implement it (measured), and the tRPC docs list Standard Schema among accepted validators. Adapters were needed before this interface existed.

q: The Orders API is called by your own React back office, a partner's Java service and an Android app in Kotlin. Which way of sharing types fits?
options: tRPC, because it removes the need to write any schema
An OpenAPI document, with a generated client per language
A shared npm package of TypeScript types that every client installs
A hand-written description of each endpoint, kept in a wiki
explain: OpenAPI is language-neutral, so every client can generate code from the same contract, and the document doubles as public documentation. tRPC's types travel through TypeScript imports, which a Java or Kotlin client cannot use. A shared TypeScript package has the same problem, and a wiki drifts from the code.

q: With strict on, why does this compile?
options: strict types every rejection reason as Error, so the read is checked
tsc infers the type of error from the errors chargeCard can throw
error is unknown, and reading nested properties on an unknown value is allowed
Its parameter is typed any: the strict catch rule covers only catch clauses
explain: The flag only covers catch clauses. The lib types a rejection reason as any, so measured, error.whatever.deep compiled inside .catch, and a network error without response would crash the handler. Prefer await inside try/catch, or annotate (error: unknown). TypeScript has no checked exceptions to infer from.

q: chargeCard can fail because the card is declined or because the payment provider times out. Which design would you approve?
options: Throw a typed exception for both and list them in a TSDoc @throws comment
Return the declined card as a value; throw on the timeout with a cause
Return null for both failures and log the reason at warning level
Return a Result for both, and for every database and network failure too
explain: A declined card is an expected outcome the caller must handle (tell the customer), so it belongs in the return type. A timeout is an incident: throwing it with cause lets retries, the error middleware and alerting deal with it. TypeScript cannot type thrown exceptions, so a comment is not enforced; returning Result for every infrastructure failure clutters every call site.
